summary: This document specifies an updated format for Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash Identifiers, replacing the one in RFC 4843. These are IPv6-looking identifiers derived from cryptographic hashes, meant for applications and APIs as endpoint identifiers rather than as network locators.

plainLanguage.summary: ORCHIDv2 identifiers look like IPv6 addresses but identify endpoints rather than network locations. RFC 7343 defines how to build them from an input, a usage context and a selected cryptographic hash algorithm.

questions: cryptographic hash identifiers as ipv6 addresses
what is the orchid ipv6 prefix
subtitle: An IPv6-shaped identifier format that binds a cryptographic hash to an endpoint identity and usage context.

tldr.problem: Applications needed hash-based endpoint identifiers that could pass through existing IPv6 APIs, and the earlier ORCHID format could not identify which hash algorithm was used.
tldr.mechanism: ORCHIDv2 combines a fixed 28-bit prefix, a 4-bit algorithm ID and 96 bits from a hash of a Context ID followed by an input bitstring.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7343 replaces RFC 4843 with a new ORCHID prefix and algorithm identifier. It has been updated by RFC 9374.

today: RFC 7343 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2014. It obsoletes RFC 4843 and has been updated by RFC 9374.

sections.title: Identifiers Rather Than Network Locations
sections.content:
Overlay Routable Cryptographic Hash Identifiers (ORCHIDs) are address-shaped identifiers intended to be statistically unique and securely bound to an input bitstring and a context. They identify endpoints at applications and APIs, rather than locations in IP headers.

ORCHIDs are non-routable at the IPv6 layer but may be routed by an overlay. The format is intended to let existing IPv6 applications carry these identifiers without treating them as ordinary IP locations.
sections.plainLanguage: An ORCHID names an endpoint, not its network location. An application can carry it like an IPv6 address while an overlay handles delivery.

sections.title: Why ORCHIDs Have a Separate Prefix
sections.content:
A separate IPv6 prefix helps applications distinguish ORCHIDs from regular IPv6 addresses. It also lets network operators block the prefix at the IP layer. The RFC says coordination is important because an uncoordinated use could conflict with a later assignment of that prefix.

The earlier ORCHID format lacked cryptographic algorithm agility. ORCHIDv2 places an index for the algorithm suite inside the identifier, and IANA allocated a new prefix because the updated format is not backward compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: A reserved prefix keeps ORCHIDs distinct from ordinary IPv6 addresses. ORCHIDv2 also identifies its hash algorithm so a context can adopt another algorithm later.

sections.title: How an ORCHIDv2 Value Is Built
sections.content:
The ORCHID Generation Algorithm takes an input bitstring and a 128-bit Context ID. It concatenates the context and input, hashes the result, extracts the middle 96 bits, then adds a 28-bit prefix and a 4-bit OGA ID. The final identifier is 128 bits.

The Context ID identifies the usage context and its hash rules. Each context defines which hash function its OGA ID values select. The input is expected to be unique or statistically unique within that context.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm combines a context and an input, hashes them, and keeps the middle 96 hash bits. A fixed prefix and a 4-bit algorithm ID complete the 128-bit identifier.

sections.title: Routing and Forwarding
sections.content:
ORCHIDs are endpoint identifiers, not locators for IPv6 routing. Routers may be configured not to forward packets with an ORCHID source or destination, and may return an ICMP administratively prohibited message for a destination ORCHID.

Router software must not add special handling code for ORCHIDs. If a network blocks them at the IP layer, it does so through configuration, such as an access-control rule for the prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers do not need special ORCHID code. An operator can block the reserved prefix with a normal configuration rule.

sections.title: Hash Choice and Security Requirements
sections.content:
The format reserves as many bits as possible for the hash while allowing multiple usage contexts to share the namespace. It puts the Context ID into the hash input rather than the identifier itself. The OGA ID gives each context a way to identify its hash function.

All mechanisms using one Context ID must generate identifiers by the same rules, or an attacker could cause a weaker hash choice to affect the context. Each method must also make input bitstrings unique or statistically unique. The RFC cites counters, pseudorandom values with at least 96 bits of entropy, or randomly generated public keys as examples.
sections.plainLanguage: Every system using one context must follow the same generation rules. The input also needs enough uniqueness so two entities are unlikely to receive the same identifier.

sections.title: The ORCHIDv2 Allocation
sections.content:
IANA allocated the 28-bit prefix 2001:20::/28 for ORCHIDv2 from the IPv6 Special Purpose Address Block. The earlier temporary prefix for experimental ORCHIDs was returned to IANA in March 2014.

This RFC does not assign a Context ID. Context IDs use the existing CGA Type Tag namespace, where new values follow First Come, First Served rules; this document requires no IANA action for them.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA reserved 2001:20::/28 for ORCHIDv2. Each application defines its own context identifier under the existing allocation rules.

sections.title: Binding the Identifier to Its Input
sections.content:
The binding between an ORCHID and its context and input depends on the hash function's second-preimage resistance. The 4-bit OGA ID identifies a hash function within its context; each context defines its own OGA ID meanings.

The hash output is truncated to 96 bits. The RFC points out that security considerations for hash truncation also apply to ORCHIDv2. It further requires each usage method to ensure that its inputs are unique or statistically unique within the context.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier's security depends on the chosen hash and on unique inputs. Because the hash is shortened, the RFC's hash-truncation security considerations apply.

fields.name: OGA ID
fields.desc: Identifies the hash algorithm within the usage context.

fields.name: Hash portion
fields.desc: Middle 96 bits from the hash of the Context ID and input.
